positioning: America's working cat made good. A hardy, easygoing all-rounder.
story: The American Shorthair earned its place the hard way. Its ancestors came over on ships with the first European settlers, brought along to protect food stores from rats and mice. For generations they were simply the sturdy working cats of farms, barns, and homes across the country.

Fanciers eventually recognized that this hardy native cat deserved a standard of its own, and developed it into a breed while keeping its rugged good health. The result is a solid, muscular, medium-to-large cat with a broad face and a dense coat, the classic silver tabby being the best known.

The temperament is the breed's calling card. American Shorthairs are easygoing, adaptable, and friendly, equally happy to play or to settle in beside you. They get along with children, dogs, and other cats, and they tolerate change with unusual grace.

They are also famously healthy and long-lived, a legacy of generations of natural selection as working cats. CFA recognized the breed in 1906, originally as the Domestic Shorthair, and it remains one of America's favorite cats.

The American Shorthair earns its keep as the low-maintenance family cat. It is adaptable and undemanding, equally at home with children, dogs, and quiet retirees, and it takes the comings and goings of a busy household in stride. A weekly brush is about all the coat asks.

Its working-cat heritage shows in robust health and a long life, often into the high teens. The main risks are a tendency to put on weight without enough play and, as in many breeds, a chance of the heart condition HCM, so measured meals, active games, and regular checkups keep it thriving.
fblocks: The shorthaired working cat of America, formalized from the country's everyday house and barn cats.
Descended from cats carried on ships to control rodents, prized for centuries for hardiness rather than looks.
Adaptable and tolerant, it suits families, other pets, and busy homes. Easy to groom and generally robust, though it can gain weight if overfed.
A short, thick, hard coat in many colors and patterns, with the silver classic tabby the signature look.
Recognized by CFA in 1906, originally as the Domestic Shorthair. Known for long life and sturdy health.
Easy on every front. Brush weekly, keep it playing, and it fits almost any home and any age of owner.
Hardy and long-lived, but prone to weight gain and, in some lines, the heart condition HCM, so manage diet and screen where possible.

last_walk:
The porch light comes on as the sky turns gold.
The American Shorthair has crossed puddles, inspected boots, and claimed every patch of sun this week. Now it waits on the porch, calm and alert, as the snow gives way to mud and a hint of spring. A working cat at the end of a good day.
